title: Purim
lead: Purim, "Lots," is the Jewish feast of the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar, set up in Esther 9 to remember how the Jews of Persia were saved from Haman's decree. It is kept with the public reading of the scroll of Esther, feasting, gifts of food and gifts to the poor.

sections.b: The name comes from pur, a word borrowed from Akkadian puru, "lot," which the book explains in Hebrew: "Pur, that is, the lot" (Esther 3:7; compare Esther 9:24–26). Haman cast it to pick the day of destruction; the Jews keep the day of their rest instead. Esther 9:17–32 sets the dates (the fourteenth of Adar in the villages, the fifteenth in walled Susa), and Mordecai's and Esther's letters bind the Jews and their descendants to keep it. 2 Maccabees 15:36 calls it "Mordecai's day." Josephus describes it (Antiquities 11.292–295). The Mishnah tractate Megillah regulates the reading of the scroll. Purim is not one of the feasts of the law of Moses (Leviticus 23); it is the one feast in the Hebrew Bible set up outside the land, for Jews living among the nations.
